title: Recording "Margie" and recording bands
summary: They rehearsed "Margie" in a theater dressing room and recorded it for Decca before playing it on a job; Andy Kirk was another good recording band.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: you decided the arrangement of "Margie" did you record it? How long after (inaudible).

About a month or so, not long after because I remember we first rehearsed it in -- we first rehearsed the arrangement in the -- in a theater there in New York down on Broadway. I can't think of the theater. It wasn't the Fairmount. Loew's State Lowenstein -- upstairs in a dressing room -- we first rehearsed it up there. And we never did play it out on a job. We recorded it before we ever did play it out anywhere on a job.

Most guys liked to play a tune out on a job about a week or so before they recorded it, but we never did record that -- play that out on a job before we recorded it. I think we did that for Decca. I'm pretty sure we did when I was with
him. But we did that -- we did a lot -- we did a lot of tunes then for Decca, then he did a lot for Columbia later on, Lunceford did.

But I don't know. I enjoyed recording with that band because they worked hard. They got the song right, you know, before they would really record it. And it was a good recording band. That's something you have to work at, recording. A lot of bands play good, don't record good. And that's a -- that's strange, isn't it.

But I'll tell you another good recording band to me back there then was Andy Kirk. I thought he had a fine recording band especially when he had Pha Terrell singing with him like -- things like "Until the Real Thing Comes Along" and things of that sort. The band sounded mellow, you know, really caught on in the studios.
